text.p: Timberland Co. reported record fourth-quarter profits Thursday, but executives warned the footwear and clothing maker would have trouble making a profit in the first half of 1997, and the company's stock plunged.

Timberland -- known for its hiking boots and grunge-style clothing -- reported fourth-quarter net income of $11.4 million, or 99 cents a share for the quarter ended Dec. 31, 1996, compared with $759,000, or 7 cents a share, in the same period in 1995.
The Stratham, N.H.-based company also notched a record for revenues, reporting sales of $221 million for the quarter vs. $175.8 million in the year-ago quarter.
But Timberland stock lost 8 percent of its value, plummeting $3.75 to $43 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trading. It was the biggest loser on the exchange.
The plunge followed a warning by Timberland Chief Financial Officer Keith Monda that it would be hard for the company to follow up the record quarterly net income with a first-half profit this year.

"Given our strong seasonality and the increasing percentage of retail business, with the higher level of retail costs, it is difficult to achieve a profit in the first half of the year," Monda told analysts and reporters in a conference call.
Chief Operating Officer Jeffrey Swartz said a focus in 1997 will be enhancing and "cleaning up" Timberland's distribution programme by moving to a higher-quality but smaller network.

"Eliminating unprofitable, non-brand-enhancing distribution is a strong signal to consumers and shareholders at the same time that this company is willing to endure short-term revenue losses in certain markets in order to ensure the long-term growth and power of the Timberland brand," he said.

Timberland -- which has gone beyond its line of rugged footwear into casual men's and women's footwear, as well as children's shoes -- will renovate and expand its New York City store this year and will add to its string of 71 owned and operated stores, Swartz said.
The company will narrow the number of department stores it serves to fewer, higher-quality stores, he said.

Swartz said Timberland also will continue to improve its operations, which have hindered the company's strong sales in the past. Timberland has strengthened management and cut the number of distribution centres, he said.

"We still turn our inventory (over) less effectively than our competitors," he said. "Our lead times are still long, and our ability to forecast demand for our products (is) less capable than it needs to be."

Fourth-quarter sales were driven by a $48 million rise in domestic sales to $175.8 million, compared with the year-ago quarter. That more than offset a drop of $2.7 million to $45.3 million in international sales, Monda said.
Worldwide apparel and accessory revenues rose $14.8 million from last year to $58.5 million in the fourth quarter, he said.
Timberland's bottom line also benefited from lower manufacturing costs, some of it due to a 1995 restructuring, and fewer sales returns, Monda said.
For the year, Timberland had net income of $20.4 million, or $1.81 a share, on revenues of $689.9 million, vs. a loss of $11.6 million, or $1.04 per share, on revenues of $655.1 million in 1995.

The 1995 loss included two one-time items: a pretax charge of $16 million for the restructuring and a pretax gain of $12.1 million for the appointment of Inchcape Plc as Timberland's Asia-Pacific distributor.
